Changing allocation to p_terminal=0.75 does not automatically change the objective weights: separately normalized branch means still carry coefficients 0.5 each. With fixed, positive branch counts and unbiased within-branch means, allocation changes gradient variance only. Approximately, Cov(ĝ)=¼(Σ_T/n_T+Σ_R/n_R): more terminal examples reduce terminal variance while fewer reconstruction examples increase reconstruction variance; total variance need not improve. This follows from standard [stratified-gradient estimation](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/lu21d/lu21d.pdf).

For independent Bernoulli assignment of B examples, counts are random. If empty branches contribute zero and nonempty branch means are conditionally unbiased, direct calculation gives E[ĝ]=½[1−(1−p)^B]g_T+½[1−p^B]g_R. At p=0.75, reconstruction is absent with probability 0.75^B, versus 0.25^B for terminal. Thus allocation changes both variance and finite-batch effective weighting through branch presence; it does not create explicit 0.75/0.25 loss weights. Random counts also introduce inverse-count variance and branch-presence fluctuations. Fixed nonzero quotas eliminate this absence effect.

Variable masked-target counts require a separate distinction: pooling all target losses estimates a target-weighted objective, whereas averaging each sequence’s mean estimates a sequence-weighted objective. The pooled mean is a random ratio and can have finite-batch bias relative to the population target mean when target count relates to loss or gradient; changing allocation can change that bias. Random denominators alone do not prove bias if conditional target means remain constant. See the primary study [The Ratio Bias in Surveys](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2281815). Consequently, specify the intended averaging unit and handle zero-target branches before claiming allocation changes variance alone.
